name: Sumerian
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Jagersma, Abraham Hendrik (Bram). 2010. A descriptive grammar of Sumerian. PhD dissertation, Universiteit Leiden. xxv+747 pp. hdl.handle.net/1887/16107 (open-access PDF from scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl).
catalog_locator: §3.11 'Stress', pp. 63-67; the quoted passage at pp. 65-66; exceptions caveat p. 67; domain sentence §4.3.3 'Phonological word', p. 72
catalog_quote: What, then were the stress rules of Sumerian when it was still a living language? The key to an answer lies in the following observation: all Sumerian loanwords in Akkadian are stressed on the last syllable of the Sumerian word (Keetman 2005: 2 note 7). This suggests that all Sumerian words were stressed on the last syllable, which would put Sumerian among the circa 10 per cent of the world’s languages that have fixed stress on the last syllable in each word (Goedemans & van der Hulst 2005: 62). [...] In all early Akkadian loanwords from Sumerian, the stress in Akkadian falls on the syllable that was the final syllable in the original Sumerian word. Why would that be so? I can see only one explanation: The original Sumerian word was stressed on the final syllable and this stress was retained in the Akkadian loanword. [...] These early loanwords do not only show that Sumerian words were stressed on the final syllable, but also prove that syllable weight played no role in the placement of Sumerian stress. The loanwords from the third group demonstrate that also Sumerian words with a final vowel were stressed on the final syllable, even though the final vowel of most if not all of these Sumerian words was short.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sumerian (as a living language, 3rd millennium BC) is reconstructed as having a stress-accent (weaker than German, like Italian/Spanish) fixed on the final syllable of every phonological word, regardless of syllable weight or vowel length; the evidence is that every early Sumerian loanword in Akkadian is stressed on the syllable that was word-final in Sumerian (final consonants are geminated in Akkadian to make that syllable heavy). Inflected forms (unnedukku < ù-na-a-du11.g) and forms with enclitics follow the same rule: when a clitic (genitive {ak}, other case markers, possessive {ane}) is added, stress moves rightward onto it, which explains initial-syllable loss in eden-na > dè-na, iti-da > ti-da, ama-ar-gi4 > ma-ar-gi8.
new_statements.exceptions: Not every clitic/suffix necessarily attracted stress: the final vowels of a few case markers and the ordinal suffix were lost in some forms, so those must have been unstressed. Earlier views differ: Falkenstein 1959b (strong expiratory accent, initial stress inferred from syllable loss) and Krecher 1969 (weight-sensitive stress read off plene/geminate spellings in OB non-standard orthography) are reviewed and rejected by Jagersma as based on unreliable criteria or on Akkadianised OB texts. Zólyomi 2017: 33 hedges ('probably stressed on the last syllable').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the phonological word (stem + suffixes + enclitics); the rule is reconstructed from loanword stems (citation forms) plus one inflected loan and vowel-loss patterns; the script never marks stress. Reconstruction of an extinct language, not observation.
new_statements.identity_note: Extinct language (sux, sume1241); every statement is a reconstruction. Jagersma's final-stress rule is for Sumerian as a living language (3rd millennium BC, Old/Neo-Sumerian corpus, main dialect Emegir); Krecher's competing weight-sensitive rules concern Old Babylonian-period Sumerian in non-standard orthography written by Akkadian scribes, which Jagersma argues may reflect Akkadian stress. The Emesal sociolect is not treated for stress in any source read.

sources.note: Dedicated section: Sumerian had a stress-accent (not as strong as German); from the accentuation of all early Sumerian loanwords in Akkadian, stress fell on the last syllable of every word, weight played no role; enclitics (genitive {ak}, case markers, possessive {ane}) attract the accent rightward; §4.3.3: 'Primary stress goes on the last syllable in each word'. Reviews and rejects Falkenstein 1959b (initial stress) and Krecher 1969 (weight-sensitive).
